chapters.title: The Obstacles of the Craving Spirits

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: What kind of obstacles do these craving spirits have? Slide nine. They have outer obstacles that prevent them from getting what they want, or from being able to partake of it. For example, they're constantly thirsty. And then they finally see water — it's raining — and they run outside. But as they run toward the water, evil monsters beat them back; they can't get outside. Or when they reach the water source, the water is no longer water — it's turned into pus and blood. Or they think, "I'm hungry," but all the donut shops are locked. When will they open? On Monday. But they live in a world that is always Sunday. They wake up every morning to get a donut, and it's Sunday again. And they never get to Monday. They see the people in the donut shop making donuts for Monday, but it never becomes Monday. That's in scripture. Just kidding. But seriously — that's a particular kind of suffering. It's always Sunday and it never gets to Monday. Or you constantly have to work, and it's always Friday and never Saturday: you go home from work on Friday, "oh, I finally have a weekend," and then you wake up on Friday again and have to go to work. Next slide, slide 10.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The second type of craving spirit has inner obstacles. They might have really tiny mouths but huge bellies, so they can never get enough food into their mouths. It's a really good picture, right? This is one of my favorites — no ChatGPT for this one, I made this one myself. Or their throats are really, really tiny. Or no matter how much food they put in, they're never full. It's like you can never be satisfied. Third type, next slide. They have the obstacle that whatever they eat or drink leaves them unfulfilled. Or they eat food and it turns into fire and burns their insides — it scorches their whole esophagus.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: There's a reason I keep choosing pictures of humans. We keep saying these are craving spirits — I mean, we're talking about the causes of becoming a craving spirit, which is true. But you can already see the behaviors in people before they become one. They're not even capable of practicing the Dharma — meaning they're not even capable of thinking of these ideas. People overcome with addiction, conflict — constantly going to the casino, or drinking, or pornography, whatever it is. It prevents them from even thinking about these ideas. Or people obsessed with money: "I've got to get my Bitcoin." The stupidest thing in the universe. Its value is based on what? Nothing. People lose more on Bitcoin every year than the people who make money on it. It's just legalizing gambling. But you can see the obsessions people have, and what they're going to lead to.

chapters.title: Don't Judge Others' Karma — Look at Your Own

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But I'll say one thing: stop judging other people. Don't go around saying, "oh, that one's going to be a craving spirit, that one's going to be an animal," and so on. We know people who like to karma-blame others: "oh, that's your bad seeds." Have you heard that before? "Oh my God, you're going to the hell realms because you're such a bad person." Don't worry about other people's good and bad karma. Worry about your own. That doesn't mean that if people are doing bad things you don't care — you've got to be judicious about it, and you might need to help them. But when you study the Vinaya really carefully, the way you help people is not by walking up to them and saying, "that's bad karma, you should stop that." "Oh, I'm going to write you an email and tell you all about it." That's not how you help people. No — it's gentler than that.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And you have to look at your own karma. Because, like I said earlier, you might think someone's hurting you, but they might be loving you, and you're just seeing it that way because of how you've treated others in the past. I ended a relationship because I thought the person was hurting me. It was awful — a terrible experience. And then three months later we hung out, and it turned out they were trying to help me. I was like, "that just does not compute." So look at your own karma first. Because how did I change that situation with that ex-partner? What I saw, I learned. I realized, "that's coming from me, and I need to change that." I did tong-len [GTONG LEN]. I'll tell you about that some other time. But I changed the karma completely. And then you ask yourself the weird question — because afterward they told me they were helping me: did I change the karma so that they were actually helping me from the start? Or did I just change the karma afterward, so that looking back I see them as helping me, when at the time they really were hurting me? You've got to think about it. You can change the past if you purify it. One of your greatest enemies in the past could become your greatest teacher. The person you think is hurting you could be loving you. It doesn't mean that, in the moment you experience them hurting you, it's not real. You have to be subtle, subtle, subtle. Let's pause there.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt

Like you never get to go home — it's always going to be Monday in Taiwan. You don't get to go home, Tim — you have to stay here forever. She's going to talk about the Bodhisattva vows now.
